title: 道德經 第四十五章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 45, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 75. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 45 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 洪德 (Vast Potency). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
大成若缺，
其用不弊。

morph.gloss: great — here 'the greatest kind of'
completion, a thing carried through to the end
to be like, to look like — it does the work English needs 'seems' for
a chip, a gap, a piece missing — what is broken off or left out
its
use, putting to work — what it is good for
not
worn out, threadbare — to go to rags, to fail with use

sentences.l:
Great completion, like a piece missing;
its use not worn out.
sentences.i: The greatest completeness looks as if a piece were missing, and putting it to use never wears it out.
sentences.n:
The chapter is one frame said five times: 大 X 若 Y — the greatest X looks like its own opposite — and then 其用不 Z, and its use never gives out. Read the five as one sentence; no single member is the point.

若 is 'to be like', and it is carrying the weight English puts on 'seems': there is no verb 'to be' here and none is wanted. 大成若缺 is four characters — great, completion, like, missing — and nothing else.

缺 is a physical word: the chip out of a jar's rim, the notch, the piece not there. What is finished to the last degree has an unfinished look, and that is why it does not wear out: nothing has been closed off, so nothing can be used up. On the standard rhyme-group analysis 缺 and 弊 belonged to the same Old Chinese rhyme class, so the couplet chimed; Mandarin quē / bì has lost it.

sentences.t:
大盈若沖，
其用不窮。

morph.gloss: great — here 'the greatest kind of'
fullness, being filled to the brim
to be like, to look like — it does the work English needs 'seems' for
hollow, empty (standing for 盅, an empty vessel); Wang Bi glosses it 虛 'void'
its
use, putting to work — what it is good for
not
to come to an end, to run out, to be exhausted

sentences.l:
Great fullness, like a hollow;
its use not exhausted.
sentences.i: The greatest fullness looks hollow, and there is no end to the use of it.
sentences.n:
Chapter 4 opened with 道沖而用之或不盈 — the Way is a hollow, and use it as you may it never fills. Here the same two words come back the other way round: what is full to the utmost looks like the hollow. The book keeps turning this pair over, because a vessel that is already full has no use left in it and a hollow one has nothing but use.

This couplet you can still hear: 沖 chōng and 窮 qióng rhymed in Old Chinese and rhyme in Mandarin. Where the earlier pair's chime is gone, this one survives.

sentences.t:
大直若屈，
其用不居。

morph.gloss: great — here 'the greatest kind of'
straightness, being straight and true
to be like, to look like — it does the work English needs 'seems' for
a bend, a giving way — to be crooked, to double back
its
use, putting to work — what it is good for
not
to settle, to lodge, to take up a fixed place

sentences.l:
Great straightness, like a bend;
its use does not settle.
sentences.i: The greatest straightness looks bent, and its use never settles in one place.
sentences.n:
Wang Bi comments on the first half: it goes straight along with each thing, and its straightness is not lodged in any one of them, so it looks bent. He does not gloss 其用不居, but 居 — to dwell, to take up a fixed place — says of the use what 不在一 says of the straightness, and the two lines then read as one thought about anything that adapts: fitted to everything, it settles into nothing. The link between the halves is ours, not his.

A word on the text. Printings of this chapter differ over how far the 其用 refrain runs. Many carry it through the first two members only and then run the last three together as a bare list. The text here keeps it in all five, and Wang Bi's commentary in this edition breaks at each one — which is why each is a sense-unit of its own. Nothing in the argument turns on it, but the chapter is a tighter machine with the refrain in.

sentences.t:
大巧若拙，
其用不輟。

morph.gloss: great — here 'the greatest kind of'
skill of hand, the craftsman's knack; contrivance, cleverness
to be like, to look like — it does the work English needs 'seems' for
clumsy, unskilful — the botcher's hand
its
use, putting to work — what it is good for
not
to break off, to leave off, to stop midway

sentences.l:
Great skill, like clumsiness;
its use does not break off.
sentences.i: The greatest craft looks clumsy, and its use never leaves off.
sentences.n:
Wang Bi: great skill follows what is so of itself in making the thing, and contrives no oddity, so it looks clumsy. 巧 is a suspect word in this book — chapter 19 wanted it cut off outright — because it means the knack that improves on things, and improving on things is what the Way does not do. Work that adds nothing of the workman's own has no visible cleverness in it, and it also has nothing in it to fail.

拙 zhuō and 輟 chuò rhyme, in Old Chinese and still in Mandarin: the second pair in this chapter you can hear without being told.

sentences.t:
大辯若訥，
其用不差。

morph.gloss: great — here 'the greatest kind of'
disputation, argument, the debater's eloquence
to be like, to look like — it does the work English needs 'seems' for
slow and halting of speech, tongue-heavy
its
use, putting to work — what it is good for
not
to be off, to go wrong, to miss the mark

sentences.l:
Great argument, like halting speech;
its use does not go wrong.
sentences.i: The greatest argument comes out halting, and it never misses.
sentences.n:
辯 is not eloquence in general: it is the disputing art of the age of the philosophers, the arguing-down of an opponent. Chapter 81 will dismiss it flatly — the good man does not dispute, the disputer is not good. Wang Bi's gloss here is the reason: great argument speaks out of the things themselves and invents nothing of its own, and speech with nothing invented in it comes out slow.

差 is the character for being off — a discrepancy, an error, a miss. Its use never goes wrong because there is nothing in it that could be wrong: it is only what was there.

躁勝寒，
靜勝熱。
清靜為天下正。

morph.gloss: restless motion, bustling about — hurried, unable to keep still
to overcome, to get the better of
cold

to overcome

clear, unclouded, as water that has settled

sentences.l:
Restlessness overcomes cold,
stillness overcomes heat.
Clear and still acts as the setting-straight of all under heaven.
sentences.i: Stir yourself and the cold is overcome; keep still and the heat is overcome. Clarity and stillness are what set all under heaven right.
sentences.n:
The chapter's five members were all about how a thing looks; the close is about what actually works. Both cures are real — you beat cold by moving and heat by keeping still — but only one of them is free. Wang Bi puts the catch in: it is when the restlessness is spent that the cold is beaten, whereas stillness overcomes heat by acting without forcing. Motion pays for its victory; stillness does not, and so only stillness scales up to all under heaven.

The last line has no verb 'to be' and does not need one: 清靜 stands as subject, 為 says 'acts as', and 天下正 is what it acts as. 正 is straightness in the moral and political sense — the setting right of what has gone crooked. 正 'straight' and 政 'government' are close in graph and in sense, and early writing uses one for the other freely, so the political reading — the setting right by which all under heaven is governed — is never far away.
